overview.text: Stanford University, legally Leland Stanford Junior University, is a private research university in California. Leland and Jane Stanford founded it in 1885 in memory of their son, and it opened in Palo Alto on October 1, 1891. Its founders envisioned a coeducational, nonsectarian school combining liberal arts with science and engineering—an approach that helped make Stanford part of the early movement toward the modern research university. Stanford’s research has since spanned fields including engineering, molecular biology, medicine, and economics. The university is also associated with controversial behavioral research: Philip Zimbardo’s 1971 prison simulation took place on campus and was stopped early after concerns arose about participants’ behavior.

key_facts.text: The university commemorates Leland Stanford Jr., who died of typhoid fever at age 15 in 1884; his parents founded the university the following year.
Its formal name is Leland Stanford Junior University. It opened on October 1, 1891, on the Stanford family’s Palo Alto property.
The founding vision included coeducation, a nonsectarian institution, and a combination of liberal arts with science and engineering.
Stanford’s characteristic early campus design features sandstone buildings, red-tiled roofs, arches, and quadrangles.
In 1971, 24 students selected from more than 70 volunteers took part in Zimbardo’s prison simulation; planned for up to two weeks, it ended after six days amid concerns about participants’ behavior.
